description: 27 famous combination mark logos explained by a brand designer: symbol and name side by side, stacked or built together, from Microsoft and Adidas to Amazon and Puma.

seo.title: 27 Combination Mark Logos Explained
seo.description: 27 famous combination mark logos explained by a brand designer: symbol and name side by side, stacked or built together, from Microsoft and Adidas to Amazon and Puma.

intro:
A combination mark is a logo that puts a symbol and the brand name together. The Microsoft squares next to the word Microsoft, the adidas bars above the word adidas and the Amazon smile under the word amazon are all combination marks. It is the most common type of logo, because it gives a brand a name people can read today and a symbol that can work alone later.

Logo design quick course: this guide is part of my series on logo types. Read the others on pictorial marks, emblem logos, script logos, mascot logos, wordmark logos, lettermark logos, monogram logos and abstract logos, or start with the overview of all types of logos.

What is a combination mark?

A combination mark joins two parts: a wordmark (the name set in type) and a symbol, which can be a picture, an abstract shape or a mascot. The two parts are designed to work together, but they are also designed to be used apart. That is the key difference from an emblem.

In an emblem, the name sits inside the shape and can't be separated, like the Harley-Davidson shield or the Starbucks badge before 2011. In a combination mark, you can lift the symbol out and use it alone as an app icon, a favicon or an embroidered patch, the way Lacoste uses its crocodile on shirts.

Three ways to combine a symbol and a name

Every combination mark in this article falls into one of three layouts.

Side by side: the symbol sits to the left (or right) of the name, as with Microsoft, Spotify, Slack and Chase. This horizontal lockup suits websites, app headers and shop signs, which are all wide spaces.

Stacked: the symbol sits above the name, as with adidas, Rolex, NBC and Mastercard. A stacked lockup fits square and tall spaces like packaging, watch dials and social media profile pictures.

Built into the name: the symbol touches or grows out of the letters, as with the Amazon smile, the Pizza Hut roof and the Puma cat leaping off the A. These are the hardest to design and the most memorable, because name and symbol read as one picture.

Why most brands choose a combination mark

A symbol alone means nothing on day one. Nobody knew what a swoosh or an octagon stood for until years of advertising taught them. A name alone works everywhere, but it is hard to fit into a small square. A combination mark solves both problems: the name builds recognition while the symbol earns its place.

Once the symbol is famous, a brand can drop the name. Nike started using the Swoosh on its own in 1995, Starbucks removed the words from its siren in 2011 and Mastercard dropped its name from the circles in 2019. All three began as combination marks.

Lockups: one logo, several versions

A combination mark is really a small system. Designers call each arrangement of symbol and name a lockup, and a good identity includes several: a horizontal lockup for websites, a stacked lockup for square spaces, the symbol alone for icons and the name alone for places where the symbol is too detailed. Toyota, for example, uses its ovals next to the name on dealerships and the ovals alone on the cars.

Below are 27 famous combination marks in three groups of nine: symbol beside the name, symbol above the name and symbol built into the name. Each one has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation.

logoResearch.name: Microsoft
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Microsoft introduced its four-square logo in 2012, its first new logo in 25 years.
observations: Four coloured squares form a window next to a grey wordmark set in Segoe.
The colours stand for the range of Microsoft's products, and the squares work alone as an app tile.

logoResearch.name: Spotify
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon founded Spotify in Stockholm in 2006, and the green was made brighter in 2015.
observations: Three curved sound waves sit inside a green circle beside a rounded wordmark.
The circle alone is the app icon, so the name can drop away on a phone.

logoResearch.name: Slack
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pentagram replaced Slack's hashtag logo with a pinwheel of speech bubbles in 2019, cutting its colours from 11 to 4.
observations: Four coloured shapes turn around a centre next to a bold lowercase wordmark.
The pinwheel is a hashtag in disguise, so the old symbol lives on.

logoResearch.name: Airbnb
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Airbnb launched its Bélo symbol in 2014, designed with DesignStudio in London.
observations: A single looping line draws a pin, a heart and the letter A next to a lowercase wordmark.
The pink line and the pink name feel like one piece, even though they can be split.

logoResearch.name: Chase
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Chermayeff & Geismar designed the Chase octagon in 1961, one of the first abstract symbols used by an American bank.
observations: A blue octagon sits after a wide, all-caps wordmark.
The octagon has no meaning of its own, which made it easy to own.

logoResearch.name: Adobe
logoResearch.verifiedFact: John Warnock and Charles Geschke founded Adobe in 1982 and named it after Adobe Creek, which ran behind Warnock's house.
observations: A red letter A made of three shapes sits next to the Adobe wordmark.
The A is a lettermark and a symbol at once, so it also works as the company's favicon.

logoResearch.name: Domino's
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The three dots on the Domino's tile stand for the three stores the company had in 1965.
observations: A red and blue domino tile tilts beside a bold blue wordmark.
The tile is both a game piece and a pizza box seen from the side.

logoResearch.name: Lacoste
logoResearch.verifiedFact: René Lacoste was nicknamed the Crocodile in 1927, and the crocodile has been sewn onto his shirts since 1933.
observations: A green crocodile follows a thin serif wordmark in capitals.
The crocodile is so famous that it often appears on clothes without the name.

logoResearch.name: Toyota
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Toyota introduced its three-oval emblem in 1989; the two inner ovals form a T.
observations: Three overlapping ovals sit next to a wide, spaced-out wordmark.
The ovals are drawn with a brush-like stroke, so the emblem looks crafted, not mechanical.

logoResearch.name: Adidas
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Peter Moore designed the three-bar adidas Performance logo in 1990, turning the brand's three stripes into a mountain.
observations: Three slanted bars rise above a lowercase wordmark.
The bars point up and to the right, like a hill to climb.

logoResearch.name: Converse
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Converse introduced the Star Chevron in 1975 and made it the main logo again in 2017.
observations: A star and a chevron sit above a bold, wide wordmark.
The chevron points forward, so the mark reads as a star in motion.

logoResearch.name: Mastercard
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pentagram redrew the Mastercard circles in 2016, and the overlapping red and yellow circles date back to the late 1960s.
observations: Two overlapping circles sit above a lowercase wordmark.
The overlap makes a third colour, a simple picture of two sides meeting.

logoResearch.name: Rolex
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hans Wilsdorf registered the Rolex name in 1908 and the five-pointed crown as a trademark in 1925.
observations: A gold crown sits above a green serif wordmark.
Gold and deep green feel expensive, which suits the watches.

logoResearch.name: Unilever
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Wolff Olins designed the Unilever U in 2004, built from 25 small icons for the company's brands and values.
observations: A large U made of tiny pictures sits above a hand-drawn wordmark.
From a distance it is a letter, up close it is a story about the company.

logoResearch.name: Taco Bell
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Glen Bell opened the first Taco Bell in Downey, California, in 1962, so the bell is a pun on his name.
observations: A purple bell sits above the name in bold capitals.
The bell is drawn in two simple curves, so it works at any size.

logoResearch.name: Wikipedia
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Wikipedia's puzzle globe comes from a 2003 contest won by Paul Stansifer and was redrawn in 2010.
observations: A globe of jigsaw pieces with letters from many alphabets sits above the name.
Missing pieces at the top show that the encyclopedia is never finished.

logoResearch.name: NBC
logoResearch.verifiedFact: NBC first used a peacock in 1956 to promote colour TV, and the current six-feather version was designed by Chermayeff & Geismar in 1986.
observations: A rainbow peacock sits above the three letters NBC.
Each feather is a different colour, one for each division of the network.

logoResearch.name: Mitsubishi Motors
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Mitsubishi means three water chestnuts, and the three diamonds combine the crests of the Iwasaki family and the Tosa clan.
observations: Three red diamonds meet in the centre above the name.
The name describes the symbol, so the two always belong together.

logoResearch.name: Amazon
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Turner Duckworth designed the Amazon smile in 2000; the arrow runs from a to z.
observations: An orange arrow curves under the black wordmark like a smile.
The smile is also a delivery arrow, and it became the app icon on its own.

logoResearch.name: Pizza Hut
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pizza Hut brought back its red-roof logo in 2019; the roof shape comes from its early restaurant buildings.
observations: A red roof sits on top of the name in bold italic letters.
The roof makes the restaurant itself the symbol, even for people who never saw one.

logoResearch.name: Burger King
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Jones Knowles Ritchie gave Burger King its new bun logo in 2021, based on the 1969 to 1999 design.
observations: The name is sandwiched between two halves of a bun.
The logo is the product: the name becomes the burger.

logoResearch.name: Baskin-Robbins
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Since 2006, the pink parts of the Baskin-Robbins BR have hidden the number 31, for 31 flavours, one for every day of the month.
observations: A pink and brown BR sits above the full name.
Once you see the 31, you can't unsee it, which makes the logo memorable.

logoResearch.name: Tostitos
logoResearch.verifiedFact: PepsiCo refreshed the Tostitos logo in 2026, making the two people in the Ts easier to see.
observations: The two Ts are people sharing a chip, and the dot of the i is a bowl of salsa.
The scene is hidden in plain letters, so it rewards a second look.

logoResearch.name: Tour de France
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Joël Guenoun designed the Tour de France logo in 2002, with a cyclist hidden in the letters.
observations: The R is a cyclist, the yellow O is a wheel and the sun.
The handwritten name moves like a rider, which suits a race.

logoResearch.name: Doritos
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Doritos started at Casa de Fritos in Disneyland in 1964 and went national in 1966.
observations: A fiery triangle, the shape of a chip, sits behind the name.
The triangle points the way and also reads as a play button.

logoResearch.name: Goodyear
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Frank Seiberling chose the winged foot of Mercury in 1900, inspired by a statue at his home.
observations: A winged foot sits between the words GOOD and YEAR.
Mercury was the messenger of the gods, so the foot promises speed.

logoResearch.name: Puma
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Rudolf Dassler founded Puma in 1948, and Lutz Backes drew the leaping cat in 1968.
observations: A black cat leaps off the end of a heavy, blocky wordmark.
The cat jumps from the A, so the name and the symbol move together.

listIntro: The boards below show all 27 combination marks in one consistent format, grouped by how the symbol and the name are arranged.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the size or success of the company behind it.
sectionIntroductions: The horizontal lockup: the symbol sits to the left or right of the name. It fits wide spaces like websites, app headers and shop signs.
The stacked lockup: the symbol sits above the name. It fits square and tall spaces like packaging, watch dials and profile pictures.
The symbol touches or grows out of the letters, so the name and the picture read as one. These are the hardest to design and the easiest to remember.
sectionBridge: This is a visual study of combination marks, not a ranking of companies.
Look at how each symbol relates to the name, and whether it could stand on its own as an icon.
entryFallbacks: The symbol and the name work together and apart.
Notice how the logo would read on a sign, a pack and a phone screen.

findings.heading: The name carries the early years
findings.text: Microsoft, Spotify and Airbnb all spell out their names next to the symbol, so new customers learn both at once.

findings.heading: The symbol becomes the icon
findings.text: The Slack pinwheel, the Spotify circle and the Amazon smile are the app icons, with no name at all.

findings.heading: Stacked suits square spaces
findings.text: adidas, Rolex and NBC stack the symbol above the name, which fits packaging, dials and profile pictures.

findings.heading: Built-in symbols are the most memorable
findings.text: The Amazon smile, the Tostitos people and the Tour de France cyclist hide a picture inside the name.

findings.heading: Famous symbols drop the name
findings.text: Nike, Starbucks and Mastercard started as combination marks and later let the symbol stand alone.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a combination mark
checklistItems: Does the symbol work alone at app-icon size?
Does the name read clearly without the symbol?
Do the two share the same weight, corners and colours?
Is there a horizontal and a stacked lockup?
Are the spacing and sizes fixed in your brand guidelines?
logoRosterConfig.conclusionHtml:
How to design a combination mark

1. Design the name. Start with the wordmark, because the name does most of the work in the first years. Pick or draw letters that match the brand's personality, then adjust the spacing by eye.

2. Design the symbol. Make it simple enough to work alone at 16 pixels. The best symbols say one thing, like the Amazon smile or the Taco Bell bell.

3. Balance the two. The symbol and the name should feel like one family: matching stroke weights, corners and colours. Check that neither overpowers the other. A common rule is to make the symbol about as tall as the capital letters, or twice that when stacked.

4. Plan the lockups. Design the horizontal version, the stacked version, the symbol alone and the name alone, with fixed spacing between the parts. Put them all in your brand guidelines so nobody makes up a new arrangement later.

Want a logo that works together and apart?

A combination mark gives a brand a name people can read and a symbol people can remember. Designed well, it comes as a set of lockups, from a wide version for your website to a single symbol for your app icon. Microsoft, adidas and Amazon show how far that flexibility can take a brand.

faq.question: What is a combination mark?
faq.answer: A combination mark is a logo that combines a symbol with the brand name. The two parts are designed to work together and apart. Famous examples include Microsoft, adidas, Lacoste, Amazon and Burger King.

faq.question: What is the difference between a combination mark and an emblem?
faq.answer: In a combination mark, the symbol and the name can be separated and used alone, like the Lacoste crocodile. In an emblem, the name sits inside a badge or shape and can't be separated, like the Harley-Davidson shield.

faq.question: Is a combination mark good for a new business?
faq.answer: Yes. For most new businesses it is the safest choice: the name builds recognition while the symbol becomes familiar, and the symbol can be used alone as an app icon or favicon.

faq.question: What is a logo lockup?
faq.answer: A lockup is a fixed arrangement of the symbol and the name, with set sizes and spacing. Most combination marks have a horizontal lockup, a stacked lockup, the symbol alone and the name alone.

faq.question: How much does a combination mark logo cost?
faq.answer: Prices vary a lot by designer. I design a complete brand identity, including the combination mark and all its lockups, in one week for a flat $3,000.
